extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of poetry; poets and editors interested in 19th-century prosody and editorial history
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and craft-notes on Edgar Allan Poe's poems (texts + editorial notes), focusing on prosody, sound, revision history, and occasional compositional devices (e.g., acrostics). Useful for poets, critics, and students studying poetic technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness as fugitive poetry; qualities to aspire to
rubrics_metrics.description: “In our opinion, it is the most effective single example of ‘fugitive poetry’ ever published in this country, and unsurpassed in English poetry for subtle conception, masterly ingenuity of versification, and consistent sustaining of imaginative lift and ‘pokerishness.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor praises qualities that make a short/occasional poem memorable: subtle conception (original idea/imagery), masterly ingenuity of versification (technical skill in meter/rhyme), consistent sustaining of imaginative lift (maintaining an elevated, imaginative tone throughout), and a certain striking or pungent quality ('pokerishness'). Aim for these overlapping qualities to make fugitive/short lyric poetry 'stick to the memory.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alliteration and similar sounds to create melody
rubrics_metrics.description: “Much of the melody of ‘The Raven’ arises from alliteration, and the studious use of similar sounds in unusual places.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate repetition of consonantal sounds (alliteration) and placing similar sounds in unexpected positions are cited as principal means of producing melodic effect in English verse. Craft choices about sound-patterning should be intentional and varied to shape musicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied line-length and a flowing line to shape versification
rubrics_metrics.description: “In regard to its measure, it may be noted that if all the verses were like the second, they might properly be placed merely in short lines … but the presence in all the others of one line—mostly the second in the verse—‘which flows continuously, with only an aspirate pause in the middle, like that before the short line in the Sapphic Adonic, while the fifth has at the middle pause no similarity of sound with any part besides, gives the versification an entirely different effect.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast of short and long lines (and the placement of flowing lines with mid-line pauses) is a deliberate metrical device. Use a recurring long line among shorter ones and vary mid-line pauses/patterns to create distinctive rhythmic effects; study classical meters (e.g., Sapphic Adonic) for analogous techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit English-specific prosodic resources (rhyme, alliteration) for variety of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “The resources of English rhythm for varieties of melody, measure, and sound, producing corresponding diversities of effect, having been thoroughly studied, much more perceived, by very few poets in the language. … we have other and very great advantages of sound by the modern usage of rhyme. Alliteration is nearly the only effect of that kind which the ancients had in common with us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and exploit devices especially available in English—rhyme and alliteration—to achieve melodic and metric diversity. Understanding how these tools differ from classical (accentual) systems enables purposeful choices in sound and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative revision and versioning as part of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes describing drafts and revisions: e.g., ‘‘The subject, and some lines of the original version, having been suggested by the poet’s friend…’’; drafts of ‘The Bells’ existed in shorter and longer versions; Poe added lines and repeatedly revised before publication; some stanzas were later suppressed at suggestion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems often pass through multiple drafts, additions, and suppressions. Be prepared to (a) accept suggested material from collaborators, (b) add or remove lines/stanzas across versions, and (c) revise until the author/editor judges the final form appropriate for publication. Track versions and rationales for changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding acrostic/letter puzzles (compositional device)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bracketed instruction: ‘‘To discover the names in this and the following poem read the first letter of the first line in connection with the second letter of the second line, the third letter of the third line, the fourth of the fourth line and so on to the end.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For poems that conceal names or words, construct an acrostic-like device by aligning nth letters of nth lines. Ensure the letter-patterning is precise and that readers are given (or can discover) the intended reading method; guard against accidental loss of the puzzle through editing/reformatting.
